a37.speaker: Bertha Bangala Chikadza, Ecama President
a37.name: Bertha Bangala Chikadza
a37.title: Ecama President
a37.speech: "It is a new approach (the Sona) that centred on the achievements the government has made, and we needed to be made aware of those developments and he did not tell us how the government intends to deal with the current challenges."

a37.speaker: Daisy Kambalame, MCCCI Chief Executive Officer, and Lingalireni Mihowa, Oxfam Country Director
a37.name: Daisy Kambalame
a37.title: MCCCI Chief Executive Officer, and Lingalireni Mihowa, Oxfam Country Director
a37.speech: Prior to the address, expressed hope that there would be a hint at the country's policy direction, with specific measures on how to address underlying causes of economic turmoil outlined.

a37.speaker: Lingalireni Mihowa, Oxfam Country Director
a37.name: Lingalireni Mihowa
a37.title: Oxfam Country Director
a37.speech: Mentioned the need to clearly announce interventions that would be used to prop up food security and modernise agricultural productivity to revamp the economy and address vulnerabilities.

a37.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, Malawi President
a37.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a37.title: Malawi President
a37.speech: In his State of the Nation Address, acknowledged the pain Malawians had endured in the past four years of his reign, but did not make a policy announcement; instead focused on development activities happening in districts, appealing to the electorate to ensure momentum was sustained through the ballot. ; Promised to implement the long-standing plan of constructing twin towers at Capital Hill, with at least 20-storey buildings, to increase office space for ministries, departments and public institutions.

a232.speaker: Melisa Williams, USAID Mission Director
a232.name: Melisa Williams
a232.title: USAID Mission Director
a232.speech: Says the high mortality rate in developing countries is a source of great concern; notes that estimates show that over half a million women, mostly in developing countries, die each year during pregnancy; said most of these deaths could be prevented if women have access to quality care during pregnancy and childbirth ; commended Zambia for recording a decrease in maternal mortality since 2000 but however noted that the current ratio of 591 deaths per 100,000 live births is still high and more needs to be done.

a232.speaker: Melisa Williams, USAID Mission Director
a232.name: Melisa Williams
a232.title: USAID Mission Director
a232.speech: Explained that the tents will provide a clean, safe and private environment for physical exams during antenatal care and Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV activities in Zambia's rural communities ; stated that the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, commonly known as PEPFAR, provides financial and technical support to strengthen HIV prevention, care and treatment services throughout the country ; added that the US government was pleased to partner with the Zambian people by continuing to support comprehensive, quality HIV prevention, care and treatment services, including interventions aimed at reducing maternal and child mortality.

a232.speaker: Dr. Peter Mwaba, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Zambia
a232.name: Dr. Peter Mwaba
a232.title: Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Zambia
a232.speech: Said the donation has come at an appropriate time when his ministry was doing everything possible to improve on health service delivery as stated in the Fifth National Development Plan and the National Health strategic plan of the ministry; said the ministry is committed to providing Zambians with equity of access to affordable cost effective and quality health services as close to the family as possible ; thanked PEPFAR through USAID and Zambia Prevention Care and Treatment Partnership (ZPCT) for the donation ; noted that the equipment received will significantly improve on the much needed resource supplies, leading to improved health care ; added that the ministry of health acknowledges the vital role the cooperating partners play in the development of the country.

a232.speaker: ZANIS (Zambia News and Information Services)
a232.name: ZANIS (Zambia News and Information Services)
a232.speech: ZANIS reports that Ms. Williams was speaking when USAID handed over tents and various medical and laboratory equipment worth K1.5 billion kwacha to the Ministry of Health in Lusaka today.

a246.speaker: Benjamin Gahungu, economic adviser for development and statistics of the former commune of Makebuko
a246.name: Benjamin Gahungu
a246.title: economic adviser for development and statistics of the former commune of Makebuko
a246.speech: Declares that some buildings were constructed and others rehabilitated over the course of the five years; specifies that among the completed works there was the extension of two classrooms at Ecofo Rusagara and the rehabilitation of the communal office ; "We built an administrative block at Ecofo Karoba. We also supplied furniture and equipment for the meeting rooms located at Maramvya, Murenda, Rwesero and Makebuko" ; indicates that the former commune was able to build and furnish the offices of the Maramvya and Murenda zones ; "We developed the water sources of Mwumba-Karoba-Mrwa Ngundu-Musave-Rwezamenyo-Rusagara" ; indicates that latrine blocks at the Mumuri and Rusagara markets were built.

a246.speaker: Benjamin Gahungu, economic adviser for development and statistics of the former commune of Makebuko
a246.name: Benjamin Gahungu
a246.title: economic adviser for development and statistics of the former commune of Makebuko
a246.speech: Says that the construction of the Makebuko stadium is still under way, though the works have begun and are not yet finished; reports that galleries are being built at the Mwaro-Mavuvu parking area; indicates that the former commune was able to build the hill offices, notably on the hills of Muranga, Simba, Gasarara, Gasasa, Rwesero, Mwanzari, Bugumbasha and Nyamagandika ; "We are also carrying out the construction of stalls at the Mumuri market" ; indicates that the commune extended the electricity line to the centres of Bugumbasha, Mwanzari, Nyamagandika, Gasenyi and Murenda.

a424.speaker: Joseph Kabila, former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.name: Joseph Kabila
a424.title: former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.speech: Broke his silence on 23 February, from outside the country, to give his reading of the security crisis in eastern DRC, saying the solution to the conflict is not a military one; said the roots of the crisis are at once "political, social and institutional" and originate in the rupture of the political process in 2021, when his clan was excluded from power by the current head of state.

a424.speaker: Joseph Kabila, former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.name: Joseph Kabila
a424.title: former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.speech: Accused Félix Tshisekedi of having established a "tyrannical" regime, characterised by "intimidation, arbitrary arrests, summary and extrajudicial executions, repression of the opposition, censorship of the media, as well as the forced exile of numerous opponents, journalists and opinion leaders, including religious leaders"; accuses his successor of being at the origin of all the DRC's misfortunes.

a424.speaker: Félix Tshisekedi, President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.name: Félix Tshisekedi
a424.title: President of the Democratic Republic of Congo
a424.speech: On 13 February did not mince his words in accusing his predecessor, Joseph Kabila, of being behind the armed opposition to his regime.

a424.speaker: Corneille Nangaa, former president of the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) and head of the Congo River Alliance (AFC)
a424.name: Corneille Nangaa
a424.title: former president of the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) and head of the Congo River Alliance (AFC)
a424.speech: According to him, President Félix Tshisekedi made a deal with Joseph Kabila in order to accede to power under the conditions that are known.

a497.speaker: Nemera Gebeyhu, Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Nemera Gebeyhu
a497.title: Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Said that the manufacturing sector will contribute 48.4 percent in the coming ten years from export earnings from the current 13.3 percent, while agriculture will be reduced to 36.4 percent from the current 77 percent.

a497.speaker: Ten year development plan (document)
a497.name: Ten year development plan (document)
a497.speech: Projects that the manufacturing subsector of the industry sector will be the major source of foreign currency; the mining export earnings share is expected to grow to 11.3 percent from 6.9 percent; the poverty line will drop to seven percent from the current 20 percent; per capita income is expected to lift to USD 2,201 and to grow on average 8 percent every year; the agriculture sector's share of GDP will drop to 22 percent from about 33.4 percent, the service sector will take 42.1 percent from 39.2 percent and industry will expand to 35.9 percent from about 27.4 percent; agriculture's labour force will diminish to 42 percent from about 73 percent; the agriculture sector will grow by 5.5 percent, industry by 11.4 percent and service by 10.4 percent in the first five years, with manufacturing and construction growing 18.4 and 8.5 percent respectively; in the second five-year period agriculture is projected to grow 6.2 percent, industry 14.6 percent and service 10.7 percent.

a497.speaker: Nemera Gebeyhu, Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Nemera Gebeyhu
a497.title: Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Said that quarterly evaluation will be undertaken every year in the period, which will help to identify the gap and what is supposed to be corrected, or to accelerate in the area that has been achieved.

a497.speaker: Nemera Gebeyhu, Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Nemera Gebeyhu
a497.title: Deputy Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Said the investments envelope is the other uniqueness of the plan: "We will design the investments and source of finance every time," he told Capital ; said that the auxiliary documents regarding the financing envelope have already been designed.

a497.speaker: Fitsum Assefa, Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Fitsum Assefa
a497.title: Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Said that while the current ten year plan focused on private sector led development, the government will have projects that are based on deep evaluation: "In the past there was massive public investment, while it was problematic regarding to inclusiveness. In the coming year we have to grow but the financing will be lead on sustainable financing and engaged on innovative financing source unlike the previous trend" ; "The sustainable development finance source will be supported by the government revenue, financial inclusion that expands the mobilization of saving, and efficiency gain on projects. The loan that the government may receive will proceed in a prudent manner, while development assistance is also considered as part of source of development finance in the coming years."

a497.speaker: Fitsum Assefa, Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Fitsum Assefa
a497.title: Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Said that despite the development plan being crafted for ten years, the implementation process has been classified in different periods: "For instance the initial implementation period will have three years and the second phase will have one year duration."

a497.speaker: Fitsum Assefa, Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.name: Fitsum Assefa
a497.title: Commissioner of the Planning Development Commission (PDC)
a497.speech: Regarding foreign currency exchange, at the CEO Forum held on Friday December 18, hinted that the government will use a floating exchange rate that is crafted in the ten year plan.

a666.speaker: Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh, Djiboutian Minister of Economy and Finance in charge of Industry
a666.name: Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh
a666.title: Djiboutian Minister of Economy and Finance in charge of Industry
a666.speech: Stated that "Should new resources be mobilised through this partnership, modifications may be made. By signing a single document, we will be able to have a programme approach rather than a project approach." ; welcomed the good collaboration existing between Djibouti and the UNDP, which supports the government in many areas focused on socio-economic development: "Social entrepreneurship is our priority, with the aim of creating as many jobs as possible."

a666.speaker: Fatima Elsheikh, UNDP Resident Representative in Djibouti
a666.name: Fatima Elsheikh
a666.title: UNDP Resident Representative in Djibouti
a666.speech: Congratulated the President of the Republic on his inauguration at the head of the country for a new term ; recalled that the signing of this portfolio will have as its mission to respond to several projects focused on local micro-enterprises in order to mitigate the impacts of Covid-19 and recover quickly from the socio-economic crisis.

a693.speaker: Association of Chief Executive Officers of Companies (CEOrt-Roundtable)
a693.name: Association of Chief Executive Officers of Companies (CEOrt-Roundtable)
a693.speech: Said the only way for Tanzania to free itself from dependence on aid is to involve the private sector in economic activities - an argument made by leaders representing the directors of more than 200 companies in the country, at a time when Tanzania and other African nations face service challenges due to the halting of some aid from the US government.

a693.speaker: Santina Benson, Executive Director of CEOrt-Roundtable
a693.name: Santina Benson
a693.title: Executive Director of CEOrt-Roundtable
a693.speech: Said that involving the private sector in the national economy would provide a guarantee of development and of that sector's contribution to the growth of the national economy ; "That is why CEOrt has been holding debates in order to enable discussion on issues important to sustainable social and economic development in fulfilling the dreams of the Development Vision from 2025 to 2050," she said ; in her opening speech said CEOrt had recently launched a project to economically empower women in Temeke District, which helps women engaged in various economic activities to improve their income and grow their economic independence.

a693.speaker: Professor Abel Kinyondo, Economics Lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM)
a693.name: Professor Abel Kinyondo
a693.title: Economics Lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM)
a693.speech: Urged the government to consider economic growth as the foundation of sustainable development; said the country has been through difficult economic changes, from the late Julius Nyerere to the leaders who followed him, but that in the recent period Tanzania has been witnessing growth; added that in the first quarter of 2007 economic growth was 11.90 percent and continued to grow, reaching 7.70 percent in 2011, and said that growth is expected to reach between 5.4 and 5.7 percent this year ; called for a review of the tax system so that it is simple and attractive for citizens to pay tax for the country's development, though he said there are still various challenges holding back development, including corruption ; stressed that government efforts to transform the economy should involve the private sector by using available resources, and stressed the importance of investing in research to find answers to challenges in various sectors ; "Often we depend on donors to fund various research, and some of them come with their own conditions. I think it is time for the government to start funding research in areas such as agriculture in order to bring more benefit to the country," he said.

a693.speaker: Dr Donald Mmari, Director of the Research on Poverty Alleviation (Repoa) programme
a693.name: Dr Donald Mmari
a693.title: Director of the Research on Poverty Alleviation (Repoa) programme
a693.speech: Explained the importance of cooperation between the government, the private sector and the community in using available resources to bring development ; "We have many resources that have not been used properly which could play a big role in economic growth," he said ; said that previously there were strategies for growing the economy and reducing poverty ('Mkukuta') and that now is the time to use technology to grow the economy.

a917.speaker: The New York Times (report, citing lists provided to officials and humanitarian workers)
a917.name: The New York Times (report
a917.title: citing lists provided to officials and humanitarian workers)
a917.speech: Reports that the administration of US President Donald Trump has cut aid programmes for several states where it had initially promised to maintain its support, and that according to those lists Washington will stop financing programmes in Jordan, Iraq, Lebanon, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia, Afghanistan, Ecuador, the Republic of the Congo, Madagascar, Niger, Syria, Chad and Yemen.

a917.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a917.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
a917.speech: Estimates that the US refusal to provide its aid will have the greatest impact on Afghanistan, where some 2 million people, including 400,000 children, depend on food assistance, and that the Yemeni population will also be affected, where 2.4 million people benefit from humanitarian programmes.

a917.speaker: Tom Fletcher, head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a917.name: Tom Fletcher
a917.title: head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a917.speech: Declared on 13 March that Trump’s suspension of humanitarian aid to foreign countries had caused a “seismic shock”.

a972.speaker: Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade (first formal response)
a972.name: Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade (first formal response)
a972.speech: Warned that the situation could also jeopardise broader preferential access for Namibian goods under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) regime.

a972.speaker: Penda Naanda, Executive Director, Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade
a972.name: Penda Naanda
a972.title: Executive Director, Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade
a972.speech: Said the US tariffs risk creating unfair market conditions, making it more difficult for Namibian products to compete. “In response to the 21% tariffs imposed on Namibian exports to the United States, it is important to clarify that these duties are not based on the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) principle but rather on the US trade deficit with each country divided by the total value of imports from all trading partners.” ; “As a result, the implementation of these reciprocal tariffs, as outlined in a White House statement, could override existing trade agreements, including the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), and significantly disrupt trade flows.” ; Acknowledged that Namibia’s own 42% average tariff on US goods may be a factor, but noted that not all American imports face duties under the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) tariff structure. ; Further warned that the new tariffs could undermine the competitiveness of Namibian beef and fish in the US market, with higher prices likely to reduce demand.

a972.speaker: Penda Naanda, Executive Director, Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade
a972.name: Penda Naanda
a972.title: Executive Director, Namibian Ministry of International Relations and Trade
a972.speech: Added that while the ministry is exploring several strategies to mitigate the impact of the tariffs, details cannot be disclosed at this stage.

a972.speaker: Southern African Development Community (SADC)
a972.name: Southern African Development Community (SADC)
a972.speech: Has expressed serious concern following the announcement by the Trump administration on 2 April of sweeping new import tariffs, which are expected to hit SADC economies hard.

a972.speaker: Rowland Brown, economist
a972.name: Rowland Brown
a972.title: economist
a972.speech: Told The Agenda that the development is “far from ideal”. “We need to think carefully about how to respond. There are both constructive and destructive paths. But to really understand this, we must consider three interconnected themes coming from the US” – citing actions by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the evolving geostrategic relevance of global regions, and the re-emergence of tariffs as a policy tool.

a972.speaker: Rowland Brown, economist
a972.name: Rowland Brown
a972.title: economist
a972.speech: “Elon Musk is often painted as a mega-villain, which isn’t entirely fair. These budgetary cuts are driven by necessity”, highlighting the US$2 trillion budget deficit in that country. ; “This year, around 18 to 19% of America’s revenue will go towards debt servicing. A few years ago, we warned that Namibia was on a similar path. At that point, a country risks locking itself into a debt trap. What we’re seeing is the US trying to maintain its global posture in an increasingly multipolar world.” ; Added that cutting government spending is no longer optional for the US, with development programmes like USAID among the casualties, which will have a knock-on effect on nations like Namibia that rely on such funding for vital sectors. ; “People are upset with the US, but the hard question remains: why should the US taxpayer continue footing the bill for antiretrovirals in Namibia?”

a1180.speaker: Onyoti Adigo, South Sudan National Minister of Livestock and Fisheries
a1180.name: Onyoti Adigo
a1180.title: South Sudan National Minister of Livestock and Fisheries
a1180.speech: Called for transforming South Sudan's abundant livestock and fish resources into commercially viable products to boost trade, enhance food security, and drive economic growth; emphasised the need to move beyond subsistence use and invest in commercializing the country's livestock and fisheries sectors. "We have a lot of cows, livestock. Nothing is lacking." ; "But we need to reform the sector. We need to commercialize fishing. We need to commercialize livestock. If we turn it into a commercial venture, I think all of us will benefit."

a1180.speaker: Onyoti Adigo, South Sudan National Minister of Livestock and Fisheries
a1180.name: Onyoti Adigo
a1180.title: South Sudan National Minister of Livestock and Fisheries
a1180.speech: Outlined major challenges holding back the livestock and fisheries industries, including poor infrastructure, lack of energy, and inadequate facilities for processing and preserving products; said these gaps prevent South Sudan from meeting international standards for packaging and exporting meat, milk, and fish, and noted that most of South Sudan's fish is currently bought by neighboring countries like Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, where it is processed, repackaged, and sold with foreign labels. "Our problem here with the fish and livestock is that we don't have good infrastructure or electricity. Secondly, we lack investors in the fisheries sector who can process fish according to international standards." ; "If we had proper facilities for preserving and packaging fish and beef, we could export our products and earn more revenue." ; "We need facilities to process milk, beef, and fish to meet international standards so that we can compete even in regional markets like Congo."

a1455.speaker: United Nations Resident Coordinator in Mali
a1455.name: United Nations Resident Coordinator in Mali
a1455.speech: Took the opportunity to emphasise the importance of providing "support to the populations affected by these natural disasters."

a1455.speaker: Nicolas Simard, Canadian Ambassador to Mali
a1455.name: Nicolas Simard
a1455.title: Canadian Ambassador to Mali
a1455.speech: Spoke of his country's commitment in the areas of health and education in Mali's first administrative region and announced humanitarian aid of one million dollars, or nearly 437,879,840 CFA francs.

a1455.speaker: Assa Badiallo Touré, Malian Minister of Health and Social Development
a1455.name: Assa Badiallo Touré
a1455.title: Malian Minister of Health and Social Development
a1455.speech: Recalled that the floods had affected 792 households and caused six deaths in the region, and that material aid (food, shelter kits) and financial assistance had been distributed to help the victims ; also mentioned the creation of a unified social registry to better coordinate aid to vulnerable populations.

a1455.speaker: Religious and traditional notables of Kayes
a1455.name: Religious and traditional notables of Kayes
a1455.speech: Expressed their gratitude to the government for this assistance and supported the ongoing efforts to help the flood victims.

a1461.speaker: Government of Burundi
a1461.name: Government of Burundi
a1461.speech: Announced on Sunday that it will not participate in the upcoming African Union Support Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), citing disagreements over troop deployment numbers with the Somali government.

a1461.speaker: Ahmed Moalim Fiqi, Somalia's Foreign Minister
a1461.name: Ahmed Moalim Fiqi
a1461.title: Somalia's Foreign Minister
a1461.speech: Lauded the bravery and sacrifices of Burundian troops, describing their role as pivotal in combating al-Shabab and stabilizing the country: "We deeply honour the Burundian forces of AMISOM/ATMIS for their sacrifices in supporting Somalia's security and revival and fighting terrorism. Their bravery is etched in history, and Somalia remains forever grateful for their enduring legacy," Fiqi wrote in a social media post.

a1461.speaker: Willy Nyamitwe, Burundi's Permanent Representative to the African Union (statement issued by the Burundian Embassy in Addis Ababa)
a1461.name: Willy Nyamitwe
a1461.title: Burundi's Permanent Representative to the African Union (statement issued by the Burundian Embassy in Addis Ababa)
a1461.speech: Revealed that he held a phone call with Djibouti's Permanent Representative to the AU, Eybe Abdi, who chairs the AU Peace and Security Council for December 2024, to communicate Burundi's "unfortunate non-participation" and discuss possible ways forward.

a1461.speaker: Somali officials
a1461.name: Somali officials
a1461.speech: Have suggested that Ethiopian troops might be excluded from AUSSOM, with their roles potentially filled by forces from other countries such as Egypt.

a1461.speaker: Mohamed Yusuf, Somalia's Deputy UN Envoy
a1461.name: Mohamed Yusuf
a1461.title: Somalia's Deputy UN Envoy
a1461.speech: Told the UN Security Council that Somalia had secured bilateral agreements ensuring the deployment of 11,000 troops for AUSSOM: "This commitment addresses potential security vacuums while sustaining progress in the fight against al-Shabaab."

a1482.speaker: Meaza Ashenafi, Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.name: Meaza Ashenafi
a1482.title: Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.speech: Writes that reforms have been taken in the justice system, but more efforts are necessary to restore public confidence in the judiciary. She writes that the crucial, overarching mission at this time is restoring public confidence in the judiciary, a matter she stressed when elected as Chief Justice, and that since then the judiciary has embarked on engaging stakeholders in the judicial system, holding town hall meetings with 350 Federal Court judges, 3,500 professional and support staff, 400 practising lawyers and presidents of regional supreme courts. “We assessed the damage done to the rule of law and expressed our collective aspiration for the supremacy of the law and the independence of the judiciary.”

a1482.speaker: Meaza Ashenafi, Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.name: Meaza Ashenafi
a1482.title: Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.speech: Writes that the reform agenda includes the revision of court structures and the redesign of the judicial administration system, including composition and mandate of the Judicial Council and procedures for the appointment and removal of judges, and that to implement reforms successfully “we rely on international principles and standards as well as ‘good fit’ practices. To do that, we are forging alliances with international partners such as the UNDP, USAID, the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency and the Open Society Foundation.”

a1482.speaker: Meaza Ashenafi, Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.name: Meaza Ashenafi
a1482.title: Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.speech: Writes that in the case of Ethiopia “we have opted to take a less radical approach” to judicial vetting than Kenya’s “Radical Surgery”, with most judges remaining in office; the approach involves finding the right balance to avoid legal complications, disruption of much needed judicial services and screening of judges who are corrupt and grossly incompetent, through informal feedback, questionnaires to litigants, review of disciplinary complaints, systematic inspection of files and collection of data on unjustified assets.

a1482.speaker: Meaza Ashenafi, Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.name: Meaza Ashenafi
a1482.title: Chief Justice and President of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia
a1482.speech: Writes that the issue of salaries and benefits must be addressed because “Justice is not cheap, and Ethiopia, as one of the lowest paying countries, needs to address this challenge progressively and incrementally,” and that a society that is unstable and has low levels of trust is caused by the lack of faith in a fair and swift judicial system: “If citizens have no faith in the judiciary, they will have no trust in government in general.”

a1482.speaker: Andrew Jackson, seventh president of the United States
a1482.name: Andrew Jackson
a1482.title: seventh president of the United States
a1482.speech: “All the rights secured to citizens under the constitution are a mere bubble, except guaranteed to them by an independent judiciary.”

a1544.speaker: Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (cited data)
a1544.name: Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (cited data)
a1544.speech: According to the agency, over 7.9 million people, or 51 percent of the population, live below the poverty line.

a1544.speaker: Zimbabwe Poverty Assessment Report (cited study)
a1544.name: Zimbabwe Poverty Assessment Report (cited study)
a1544.speech: Reveals a troubling trajectory: poverty rose from 23 percent in 2010/11 to a staggering 49 percent in 2020, largely due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

a1544.speaker: Rev. Taylor Nyanhete, National Director of the Zimbabwe National Council for the Welfare of Children
a1544.name: Rev. Taylor Nyanhete
a1544.title: National Director of the Zimbabwe National Council for the Welfare of Children
a1544.speech: Emphasises the strong link between poverty and food insecurity: "Poverty in Zimbabwe is intrinsically linked to food insecurity, with families, especially children, bearing the brunt" ; "A lack of disposable income leads to poor nutrition, weakening immune systems and stunting growth - both physically and mentally." He notes that these issues contribute to wider socio-economic challenges, most notably in education.

a1544.speaker: Chengeto Muzamba, resident of Msasa Park in Harare
a1544.name: Chengeto Muzamba
a1544.title: resident of Msasa Park in Harare
a1544.speech: Highlights the disproportionate impact of poverty on women: "Single mothers bear the brunt of poverty. Many struggle to access capital for businesses or afford daycare, forcing them into low-paying informal jobs" ; "Without financial independence, they remain trapped in cycles of hardship."

a1544.speaker: Chengeto Muzamba, resident of Msasa Park in Harare
a1544.name: Chengeto Muzamba
a1544.title: resident of Msasa Park in Harare
a1544.speech: On the barriers facing young people: "Many have innovative ideas but lack the financial backing and policy support to turn them into viable businesses."

a1544.speaker: Edgar Moyo, Minister of Energy and Power Development
a1544.name: Edgar Moyo
a1544.title: Minister of Energy and Power Development
a1544.speech: Stresses the role of energy in economic revitalisation: "Without a stable energy sector, industrialisation and growth are limited" ; "Our goal is to ensure every Zimbabwean, especially in rural areas, has access to reliable electricity. Energy access is directly linked to productivity, education, and health outcomes."

a1544.speaker: Daniel Garwe, Minister of Local Government and Public Works
a1544.name: Daniel Garwe
a1544.title: Minister of Local Government and Public Works
a1544.speech: Outlines government efforts to combat poverty through infrastructure development: "We've initiated projects aimed at improving lives sustainably." He cites the reconstruction of Mbare Musika, which will accommodate over 4,000 traders: "This initiative will create sustainable livelihoods for many families, including farmers, by fostering a supportive trading environment."

a1544.speaker: 2023 World Bank report (cited)
a1544.name: 2023 World Bank report (cited)
a1544.speech: According to the report, Zimbabwe now imports over $800 million worth of food annually.

a1544.speaker: Benson Moyo, farmer from Chiredzi
a1544.name: Benson Moyo
a1544.title: farmer from Chiredzi
a1544.speech: Emphasises modernising agriculture for sustainability: "We need consistent access to irrigation, affordable seeds, and mechanisation. If the government focuses on supporting small-scale farmers, we can revive the agricultural sector."

a1544.speaker: Dr. Witness Chikoko, social worker and academic at the University of Zimbabwe
a1544.name: Dr. Witness Chikoko
a1544.title: social worker and academic at the University of Zimbabwe
a1544.speech: Advocates on mineral wealth and corruption: "Strict transparency in mining contracts and fair revenue-sharing can turn these resources into national assets."

a1544.speaker: Dr. Witness Chikoko, social worker and academic at the University of Zimbabwe
a1544.name: Dr. Witness Chikoko
a1544.title: social worker and academic at the University of Zimbabwe
a1544.speech: "Education is the most powerful tool to break the cycle of poverty in Zimbabwe" ; "When people acquire knowledge and skills, they can secure better jobs, start businesses, and make informed decisions that positively impact their lives."

a1544.speaker: Alexio Mudzengeerere, founder of the Grassroots Flea Markets and Vendors Organisation
a1544.name: Alexio Mudzengeerere
a1544.title: founder of the Grassroots Flea Markets and Vendors Organisation
a1544.speech: Emphasises supporting small businesses: "For many Zimbabweans, the informal sector is their lifeline. Access to affordable loans and designated trading spaces can empower vendors and entrepreneurs."

a1633.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a1633.name: Elon Musk
a1633.title: head of the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a1633.speech: Keeps describing the American agency, which distributed American aid through partner programmes and organisations, as a "criminal organisation". He goes so far as to declare adamantly that it is "time for it to die."

a1633.speaker: OECD report
a1633.name: OECD report
a1633.speech: According to an OECD report, American aid quite simply represented one third of the American public aid that flooded the African continent in 2022 ; According to an OECD report, $1.45 billion was paid to Ethiopia in 2022.

a1633.speaker: Analysts
a1633.name: Analysts
a1633.speech: Analysts even consider that this freeze of American aid will deal a fatal blow to the fight against AIDS in Africa, so that the latest African victim of the suspension of American aid is not a country but a disease.

a1633.speaker: South African government
a1633.name: South African government
a1633.speech: Has reportedly made it clear that it would no longer tolerate the lack of respect and the contempt displayed by the Western world, after officially suspending all American companies on its territory and suspending mineral exports to the United States.

a1633.speaker: Spokesperson for the South African government (anonymous)
a1633.name: Spokesperson for the South African government (anonymous)
a1633.speech: "Africa is not a begging continent" ; "We will no longer be taken for granted. If the United States thinks it can simply cut funding and expect us to come crawling back, they are gravely mistaken." ; "We are ready to take a stand and assert our sovereignty" ; "We will no longer let ourselves be intimidated by the United States."

a1858.speaker: Omar Zniber, Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.name: Omar Zniber
a1858.title: Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.speech: Speaking on Monday before the United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC) in Geneva, called for the opening of all crossing points into the Gaza Strip in order to allow the delivery of humanitarian aid and for the safe return of displaced civilians to their places of residence.

a1858.speaker: Omar Zniber, Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.name: Omar Zniber
a1858.title: Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.speech: Recalled in this context that King Mohammed VI, in his capacity as Chairman of the Al Quds Committee, ordered the establishment of a humanitarian airlift to Gaza, which made it possible to deliver nearly 300 tonnes of humanitarian aid (food, medicines, relief supplies) via unprecedented routes, with the aim of easing the suffering of the civilian population.

a1858.speaker: Omar Zniber, Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.name: Omar Zniber
a1858.title: Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.speech: Called for respect for the historic 1967 status quo governing the Islamic and Christian places of worship in the city of Al Quds and reaffirmed Morocco's attachment to preserving the central role of UNRWA as well as that of the other Palestinian institutions responsible for humanitarian aid.

a1858.speaker: Omar Zniber, Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.name: Omar Zniber
a1858.title: Morocco's Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva
a1858.speech: Welcomed the broad international momentum in favour of recognition of the State of Palestine, which forms part of the growing support for the two-State solution, considered the most rational and the most realistic way out of the cycle of violence.

a1858.speaker: Morocco / Rabat (position stated at an Arab League meeting on 4 September)
a1858.name: Morocco / Rabat (position stated at an Arab League meeting on 4 September)
a1858.speech: Rabat had already reiterated its support for the two-State solution at an Arab League meeting on 4 September.

a1858.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1858.name: Donald Trump
a1858.title: US President
a1858.speech: Announced on Monday a 20-point plan to end the war in the Palestinian territory of Gaza; the plan provides for the "immediate" end of the war triggered in Gaza by Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023 and a phased withdrawal of Israeli forces, and stipulates that all hostages must be released within 72 hours.

a2544.speaker: Klenam et al. (2025), authors of the study "Toward Sustainable Industrialization in Africa: The Potential of Additive Manufacturing - An Overview"
a2544.name: Klenam et al. (2025)
a2544.title: authors of the study "Toward Sustainable Industrialization in Africa: The Potential of Additive Manufacturing - An Overview"
a2544.speech: Stress that deliberate policy responses are essential. These include targeted investments in technical education, incentives for AM startups, and regional platforms for knowledge sharing. "We have the opportunity to reimagine and rebuild Africa's industrial foundation in a way that is inclusive, sustainable, and resilient." - Klenam et al., 2025 ; In the words of the study's authors, additive manufacturing offers Africa a chance to "build its future layer by layer on its own terms."

a2544.speaker: Study "Toward Sustainable Industrialization in Africa: The Potential of Additive Manufacturing - An Overview"
a2544.name: Study "Toward Sustainable Industrialization in Africa: The Potential of Additive Manufacturing - An Overview"
a2544.speech: The study underscores that AM's real power lies in its adaptability to local needs. By producing goods in smaller batches, customised to specific communities or sectors, AM supports circular economies and reduces environmental impact.

a2555.speaker: Ameir Hassan Ameir, Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.name: Ameir Hassan Ameir
a2555.title: Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.speech: Explained how he will obtain the money to pay every Zanzibari 500,000 shillings a month, including by controlling the heavy spending of the government he will form, especially large presidential motorcades; said that if given the mandate the President's vehicles will not exceed six so as to reduce heavy government spending, with the money directed to projects for citizens: “Each month we will ensure we collect 1.7 trillion shillings, and by estimates the people of Zanzibar number two million, so if you distribute 500,000 shillings a month to every Zanzibari, we will use 1 trillion shillings and 700 billion will be put into the government fund for development” ; said the party will give a larger share of the collections to citizens than to government spending, because citizens are the owners of the country and its resources.

a2555.speaker: Ameir Hassan Ameir, Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.name: Ameir Hassan Ameir
a2555.title: Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.speech: Said there are nine sectors they will emphasise to grow revenue collection — tourism, fishing, organic farming, education and skills, economic infrastructure, building small and medium industries, attracting domestic and foreign investment, improving good governance and fighting corruption, and putting digital systems in place; in tourism they will grow cultural, ecological and historical tourism instead of beach tourism alone: “Increasing the quality of hotel services, transport and security for tourists and investing in new markets in Asia, the Middle East and within Africa” ; in fisheries they will invest in modern equipment and deep-sea fishing and add value to fish products through processing and packaging; in education they will produce young people in marketable fields such as technology and business and build vocational colleges: “Improving economic infrastructure, roads, electricity, clean and safe water, ports and good communication networks” ; said they will improve the investment environment by reducing bureaucracy, introducing transparency and giving incentives to investors, with domestic investors given loans at affordable interest rates.

a2555.speaker: Ameir Hassan Ameir, Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.name: Ameir Hassan Ameir
a2555.title: Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.speech: On good governance and corruption: “We will change things through actions, not words. We will put in place tough new laws; theft of public funds will be a crime of treason, its punishment will be imprisonment of not less than 15 years and confiscation of all property. Leaders found guilty will never hold office again” ; said he will ensure proper use of resources and accountability for government employees and the public and private sectors, and will introduce digital cards to control government revenue and provide services transparently, including for all car parking areas and public toilets.

a2555.speaker: Ameir Hassan Ameir, Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.name: Ameir Hassan Ameir
a2555.title: Zanzibar presidential candidate for the Makini party
a2555.speech: On the campaign assessment, said it shows Zanzibaris have received him well because of his policies and that he believes he will defeat all the other 10 candidates; said what gives him confidence is the way they have run the campaign by going to citizens in their own areas: “We go to their areas and we make sure that the very people of that area are the ones we talk to, not carrying people in vehicles and bringing them from other areas. And our policies, especially this one of giving each Zanzibari 500,000 shillings, has been very well liked.”

a2555.speaker: Fahmi Khalfan Abdalla, National Publicity Secretary of the Makini party
a2555.name: Fahmi Khalfan Abdalla
a2555.title: National Publicity Secretary of the Makini party
a2555.speech: Said every party has its own priorities, but Makini's priorities have satisfied many people, so they believe they will be elected and enter State House.

a2555.speaker: 2022 Population and Housing Census (Tanzania)
a2555.name: 2022 Population and Housing Census (Tanzania)
a2555.speech: According to the 2022 Population and Housing Census, Zanzibar has a total of 1,889,773 people.

a2602.speaker: Ibrahim Bagadoma, Governor of Diffa
a2602.name: Ibrahim Bagadoma
a2602.title: Governor of Diffa
a2602.speech: Underlined the importance of the initiative, recalling that the challenges facing the region require a collective response: “We must act together to build a better future for all.”

a2602.speaker: Displaced people at the workshop (testimonies)
a2602.name: Displaced people at the workshop (testimonies)
a2602.speech: Gave moving testimonies, sharing their experiences and their aspirations, which strengthened the participants’ determination to find concrete solutions.

a2610.speaker: UK government
a2610.name: UK government
a2610.speech: Revealed details of its plans to cut foreign aid, with support for children’s education and women’s health in Africa facing the biggest reductions; said in February it would slash foreign aid spending by 40% – from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% – to increase defence spending to 2.5% after pressure from the US ; said spending on multilateral aid bodies would be protected, including the Gavi vaccine alliance, and that the UK would also continue to play a key humanitarian role in hotspots such as Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan ; said the cuts follow “a line-by-line strategic review of aid” by the minister, which focused on “prioritisation, efficiency, protecting planned humanitarian support and live contracts while ensuring responsible exit from programming where necessary”.

a2610.speaker: Foreign Office report and impact assessment
a2610.name: Foreign Office report and impact assessment
a2610.speech: Show the biggest cuts this year will come in Africa, with less spent on women’s health and water sanitation with increased risks, it says, of disease and death.

a2610.speaker: Aid charities
a2610.name: Aid charities
a2610.speech: Have criticised the move, saying the cuts would impact the world’s most vulnerable people.

a2610.speaker: Baroness Chapman, UK minister for development
a2610.name: Baroness Chapman
a2610.title: UK minister for development
a2610.speech: “Every pound must work harder for UK taxpayers and the people we help around the world and these figures show how we are starting to do just that through having a clear focus and priorities.”

a2610.speaker: Foreign Office
a2610.name: Foreign Office
a2610.speech: Said bilateral support – aid going directly to the recipient country – for some countries would decrease and multilateral organisations deemed to be underperforming would face future funding cuts; it has not yet announced which countries will be affected.

a2610.speaker: Sarah Champion, International Development Committee chair
a2610.name: Sarah Champion
a2610.title: International Development Committee chair
a2610.speech: Criticised the move, saying it appears the cuts “will come at the expense of some of the world’s most vulnerable people”.

a2610.speaker: Monica Harding, Liberal Democrat international development spokesperson
a2610.name: Monica Harding
a2610.title: Liberal Democrat international development spokesperson
a2610.speech: Said slashing UK aid spending to its “lowest level this century will have an appalling impact on some of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable people” ; “This is only the beginning – we will see far deeper and crueller cuts next year when most of the reduction happens,” she warned.

a2610.speaker: Bond, a UK network for international development organisations
a2610.name: Bond
a2610.title: a UK network for international development organisations
a2610.speech: Said it was clear the government was “deprioritising” funding “for education, gender and countries experiencing humanitarian crises such as South Sudan, Ethiopia and Somalia, and surprisingly the Occupied Palestinian Territories and Sudan, which the government said would be protected”.

a2610.speaker: Gideon Rabinowitz, Bond policy director
a2610.name: Gideon Rabinowitz
a2610.title: Bond policy director
a2610.speech: “It is concerning that bilateral funding for Africa, gender, education and health programmes will drop. The world’s most marginalised communities, particularly those experiencing conflict and women and girls, will pay the highest price for these political choices. At a time when the US has gutted all gender programming, the UK should be stepping up, not stepping back.”

a2610.speaker: Unicef, a UN agency providing aid to children
a2610.name: Unicef
a2610.title: a UN agency providing aid to children
a2610.speech: Said the cuts “will have a devastating and unequal impact on children and women” and called the move “deeply short-sighted”.

a2610.speaker: Philip Goodwin, Unicef UK chief executive
a2610.name: Philip Goodwin
a2610.title: Unicef UK chief executive
a2610.speech: “We urge the government to adopt a new strategic approach that places vulnerable children at the heart of its aid programmes and policies… At least 25% of aid should be directed to child-focused initiatives, ensuring that children’s health, nutrition, education, and protection are prioritised.”

a2610.speaker: Street Child, British-founded charity
a2610.name: Street Child
a2610.title: British-founded charity
a2610.speech: Told the BBC that some of its work to help children get access to education in Sierra Leone, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo – where British aid has been a main backer – will come to an end because of the cuts.

a2610.speaker: Tom Dannatt, Street Child CEO
a2610.name: Tom Dannatt
a2610.title: Street Child CEO
a2610.speech: Said education was the greatest long-term builder of hope, and described reducing the support as “sad and short-sighted”: “So children who used to go to school will not go to school, and so, more children will be found roaming the streets and ploughing fields and not developing their critical faculties. Whereas they should be in school learning and having a chance to build a brighter future for themselves and for their societies, but because of these cuts by British aid for the poorest children, especially in the poorest countries, that’s not the reality anymore.”

a2610.speaker: One UK cabinet minister (anonymous)
a2610.name: One UK cabinet minister (anonymous)
a2610.speech: Admitted the public no longer supports spending on foreign aid.

a2610.speaker: Foreign Office
a2610.name: Foreign Office
a2610.speech: Confirmed that the International Development Association (IDA), the World Bank’s fund for the world’s lowest income countries, would receive £1.98bn in funding from the UK over the next three years, helping the organisation benefit 1.9 billion people.

a2622.speaker: Abdallah Kilima, Tanzania’s Director of the Department of Middle East Affairs
a2622.name: Abdallah Kilima
a2622.title: Tanzania’s Director of the Department of Middle East Affairs
a2622.speech: Speaking on October 17, 2024, noted that the meeting occurred sixteen years after a similar JPC was held in Tehran, Iran; highlighted key areas of priority for Tanzania during the discussions, including investment, energy, oil and gas, technology, as well as security and defense.

a2622.speaker: Mahmoud Thabit Kombo, Tanzania’s Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2622.name: Mahmoud Thabit Kombo
a2622.title: Tanzania’s Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2622.speech: Emphasized that economic diplomacy was the primary focus of the meeting; also mentioned that President Samia’s government has worked to facilitate smoother interactions between the two countries in various sectors ; “The Iranian Minister of Agriculture, Golamreza Nouri Ghezelcheh, has come to Tanzania with a delegation of 40 government officials and 40 private sector representatives” ; “We have come to discuss issues related to agriculture, fishing, and business. Among the Iranian businessmen, two are particularly significant and are expecting to invest between 40 million to 70 million dollars in Tanzania.”

a2622.speaker: The Chanzo (2022 analysis)
a2622.name: The Chanzo (2022 analysis)
a2622.speech: Shows that Tanzania owes a total of Sh1.48 trillion to the Islamic Republic, making Iran the country with the highest outstanding debt to Tanzania.

a2622.speaker: Mbarouk Nassor Mbarouk, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Tanzania
a2622.name: Mbarouk Nassor Mbarouk
a2622.title: Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Tanzania
a2622.speech: Informed Parliament on September 12, 2023, that the government is already assessing the possibility of opening an embassy in Tehran.

a2794.speaker: USAID Ethiopia Mission Director Sean Jones and NEBE Chairwoman Birtukan Midekssa
a2794.name: USAID Ethiopia Mission Director Sean Jones and NEBE Chairwoman Birtukan Midekssa
a2794.speech: Jointly unveiled the new USAID Ethiopia Election and Political Processes Program, which will help strengthen the capacity of NEBE officials to organize, administer, and conduct free and fair elections.

a2794.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2794.name: Sean Jones
a2794.title: USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2794.speech: “These elections belong to the Ethiopian people, and we are proud to be welcomed as a partner in supporting free and fair elections, and ensuring that the voices of Ethiopians in every corner of the country are heard as this country continues its remarkable journey.”

a2914.speaker: JSE (Johannesburg Stock Exchange)
a2914.name: JSE (Johannesburg Stock Exchange)
a2914.speech: Warned it would delist Eskom’s bonds if it did not release its interim financial report within the three months stipulated by its debt listing requirements.

a2914.speaker: Eskom
a2914.name: Eskom
a2914.speech: Announced on Sunday night that it had scheduled the announcement of its interim results for this week ; previously said it was delaying the release of the results to review the impact of the 5.23% price increase granted by energy regulator Nersa, and to allow its new board to review the financials.

a2914.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, Deputy President (statement released by the Presidency)
a2914.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a2914.title: Deputy President (statement released by the Presidency)
a2914.speech: Announced a new board at Eskom on January 20, directing it to appoint a permanent chief executive and chief financial officer within the next three months, and said the new board was part of his intervention which he said will restore Eskom as an important contributor to the economy.

a3014.speaker: Ambassador Ana Nembe, Head of the African Union Delegation
a3014.name: Ambassador Ana Nembe
a3014.title: Head of the African Union Delegation
a3014.speech: “The money is intended to respond to flood affected citizens, refugees and returnees. The AU is committed to improving the livelihood of every citizen and the affected Liberians are no exception.”

a3014.speaker: Government of Liberia
a3014.name: Government of Liberia
a3014.speech: Has described as significant and remarkable the contribution of the AU to disaster response in Liberia.

a3014.speaker: Gabriel Salee, Acting Foreign Minister of Liberia
a3014.name: Gabriel Salee
a3014.title: Acting Foreign Minister of Liberia
a3014.speech: “The AU’s gesture clearly indicates its solidarity to Africanism and people across the continent, and Liberia remains grateful to the AU for its contribution and humanitarian assistance over the years” ; Noted that the AU’s intervention will help to respond to the humanitarian needs of returnees and flood victims.

a3019.speaker: The Kremlin
a3019.name: The Kremlin
a3019.speech: Has said that Russian President Vladimir Putin may address a possible ceasefire with Ukraine on Thursday.

a3019.speaker: TASS (Russian state news agency)
a3019.name: TASS (Russian state news agency)
a3019.speech: Reported that the Kremlin said Putin may address a possible ceasefire with Ukraine on Thursday.

a3019.speaker: Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesperson
a3019.name: Dmitry Peskov
a3019.title: Kremlin spokesperson
a3019.speech: Said Mr Putin is set to take questions from reporters with his Belarusian counterpart, Alexander Lukashenko, while the latter is on an official visit to Russia. “Everything will depend on what reporters will ask,’’ Mr Peskov told TASS when asked whether Mr Putin would comment on issues beyond Minsk-Moscow relations ; On Wednesday, Mr Peskov said that Moscow would not publicly comment on the proposal discussed by the US and Ukraine until it would know all the details.

a3019.speaker: Ukrainian delegation (at the Jeddah talks)
a3019.name: Ukrainian delegation (at the Jeddah talks)
a3019.speech: Expressed willingness to agree to an immediate 30-day comprehensive ceasefire if Russia would do the same.

a3019.speaker: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and National Security Advisor Mike Waltz
a3019.name: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and National Security Advisor Mike Waltz
a3019.speech: Have promised to provide Moscow with all the information about the Jeddah negotiations.

a3019.speaker: US President Donald Trump
a3019.name: US President Donald Trump
a3019.speech: Said on Wednesday that a US delegation was on its way to Moscow ; Had also said that he would want to speak with Mr Putin by phone, soon.

a3019.speaker: The White House
a3019.name: The White House
a3019.speech: Announced that special envoy Steve Witkoff would visit Russia in a few days.

a3036.speaker: Workshop on the application of the 2013 decree banning plastic bags (final resolutions)
a3036.name: Workshop on the application of the 2013 decree banning plastic bags (final resolutions)
a3036.speech: Adopted 21 recommendations in order to have the measure applied, including: implementation of the enforcement measures provided for by the decree; continuing information and communication on the decree; creating an environmental police force for monitoring and enforcement; strengthening border controls; building the capacities of actors; setting up a platform for reporting clandestine producers of plastic bags; establishing a chain for the collection and treatment of plastic packaging under the environment code; emphasising recycling and the circular economy; setting up an eco-organisation for the plastic waste sector; creating incentives (tax credits, excellence prizes) for model companies; strengthening public-private partnerships; raising public awareness of eco-citizen behaviour; integrating environmental issues into educational programmes; involving all law enforcement forces; drafting a single decree and implementing order on the ban; consulting the needs of plastics manufacturers; carrying out an impact study of the decree's implementation; incentive measures for reusable packaging; reducing input costs and lowering taxes; and popularising the sanitation and hygiene code.

a3117.speaker: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma) data
a3117.name: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma) data
a3117.speech: Shows that severe weather characterised by heavy rains has killed 31 people and injured 382 others since the start of the 2024/25 rainfall season.

a3117.speaker: Charles Kalemba, Dodma commissioner (statement)
a3117.name: Charles Kalemba
a3117.title: Dodma commissioner (statement)
a3117.speech: In a statement on Tuesday said 22 of the deaths were caused by lightning and described the figure as deeply concerning. ; “The department advises the general public to reduce the likelihood of being struck by lightning by seeking enclosed shelter immediately when caught out in the open during thunderstorms and by avoiding seeking shelter under trees or taller objects.”

a3117.speaker: Charles Kalemba, Dodma commissioner
a3117.name: Charles Kalemba
a3117.title: Dodma commissioner
a3117.speech: Said the statistics exclude damages caused by Tropical Cyclone Chido, which affected 10 159 people, claimed 13 lives and left 29 injured.

a3117.speaker: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma)
a3117.name: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma)
a3117.speech: According to Dodma, the number of households affected by recurrent disasters such as stormy rains, strong winds, heavy rains and lightning has increased from 10 833 households in December 2024 to 31 413 this month.

a3117.speaker: James Mwale, Ntchisi District Council spokesperson
a3117.name: James Mwale
a3117.title: Ntchisi District Council spokesperson
a3117.speech: In an interview on Tuesday said 48 households whose houses were damaged due to heavy rains in traditional authorities Kalumo and Malenga over the weekend were yet to be reached with support. ; “We conducted the assessment, sent the report to Dodma and we are waiting for assistance.”

a3117.speaker: Robert Nayeja, Nsanje District Council spokesperson
a3117.name: Robert Nayeja
a3117.title: Nsanje District Council spokesperson
a3117.speech: Said 1 693 people have been affected by disasters in the district so far and Dodma has since assisted them with a 50 kilogramme bag of maize each.

a3117.speaker: Department of Climate Change
a3117.name: Department of Climate Change
a3117.speech: Has forecasted more heavy rains across the country up to Sunday, January 26 2025 with the risk of flooding in some areas.

a3272.speaker: Dr Patrick Kuma-Aboagye, Director-General of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.name: Dr Patrick Kuma-Aboagye
a3272.title: Director-General of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.speech: Announced the exercise at a media briefing in Accra, said the eligible children would be administered 600-milligram praziquantel and 400mg albendazole medicines during the exercise, explained that those medicines were donated to the GHS through the World Health Organisation and would be administered under the strict supervision of specially trained school teachers and health workers, and said it was important for all children to eat before taking the medicines to help effective absorption: "Preferably, medicines should be administered immediately after the first break or after children have been served food to ensure that all children have eaten. Therefore, all parents, guardians and caregivers should ensure their children eat before going to school."

a3272.speaker: Dr Patrick Kuma-Aboagye, Director-General of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.name: Dr Patrick Kuma-Aboagye
a3272.title: Director-General of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.speech: Said female genital schistosomiasis was a severe consequence of a schistosoma infestation that occurred in girls and women, especially in endemic areas, and stated that the condition always had significant impact on the quality of life, including causing possible infertility, menstrual disorders and recurrent urinary tract infections; indicated that it was essential to increase awareness of schistosomiasis prevention of the public; said that in Ghana schistosomiasis had an estimated country-wide prevalence of 23.3 per cent, with localised prevalence levels exceeding 50 per cent; explained that soil-transmitted helminths were most prevalent in areas with poor sanitation, inadequate hygiene practices and low socio-economic conditions, with symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhoea, anaemia, malnutrition and impaired physical and reduced cognitive development; and said it was important to eliminate schistosomiasis and control soil-transmitted helminth in Ghana in order to improve the overall health and well-being of the population.

a3272.speaker: Dr Franklin Asiedu-Bekoe, Director of the Public Health Division of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.name: Dr Franklin Asiedu-Bekoe
a3272.title: Director of the Public Health Division of the Ghana Health Service
a3272.speech: Urged the media to use their platforms to enlighten the public on the deworming exercise, raise awareness about its importance, and to encourage individuals to participate fully.

a3272.speaker: Theresa Oppong-Mensah, Director of the School Health Education Programme of the Ghana Education Service
a3272.name: Theresa Oppong-Mensah
a3272.title: Director of the School Health Education Programme of the Ghana Education Service
a3272.speech: Gave the assurance that the schools were ready for the deworming exercise, adding that they had collaborated with the Ghana School Feeding Programme to ensure that enough food was provided on the day of the administration of the medicines: "Parents have also been educated on it and they are also going to support us with water and food as well. This is to indicate that GES is ready, and we are fully in support of this exercise."

a3272.speaker: Irene Dzathor, Programme Director of the USAID Act to End NTDs Programme
a3272.name: Irene Dzathor
a3272.title: Programme Director of the USAID Act to End NTDs Programme
a3272.speech: Expressed the commitment of her outfit to the fight against schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminth elimination in Ghana.

a3681.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a3681.name: Antonio Guterres
a3681.title: UN Secretary-General
a3681.speech: Appealed on Tuesday for significant international support for Somalia as it battles a desperate humanitarian crisis caused by “a perfect storm” of drought and protracted armed conflict; said at a press conference with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud in Mogadishu that he was on a “visit of solidarity” to the Horn of Africa nation ; “This combination of terrorism and drought, largely caused by climate change, creates a perfect storm for the people of Somalia and requires massive support from the international community,” Guterres said during a visit to a camp for internally displaced people ; “The people I met have lost their livestock, they have lost their property, they have lost everything,” he told reporters in the drought-hit district of Baidoa ; said the UN's $2.6 billion call for humanitarian assistance was only 15 percent funded.

a3681.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a3681.name: Antonio Guterres
a3681.title: UN Secretary-General
a3681.speech: In a report to the UN Security Council in February, said that 2022 was the deadliest year for civilians in Somalia since 2017, largely as a result of Al-Shabaab attacks.

a3681.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of Somalia
a3681.name: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud
a3681.title: President of Somalia
a3681.speech: Said the UN chief's two-day visit, the first since March 2017, was also a gesture of solidarity “towards the government and the democratic process of Somalia” ; “This visit ensures that the United Nations is fully committed to support our plans for state building and stabilising the country,” his office said in a statement.

a3681.speaker: United Nations
a3681.name: United Nations
a3681.speech: Says about half of Somalia's population will need humanitarian assistance this year, with 8.3 million affected by the drought; according to the UN, seasonal rains in March led to flooding that claimed the lives of 21 people and displaced more than 100,000, and it warned that the rains were unlikely to be enough to improve the food security outlook for many; according to the UN, Somalia's 2011 famine killed 260,000 people, more than half of them children under six, partly because the international community failed to act fast enough.

a3681.speaker: Report by the UN and the Somali government (released in March)
a3681.name: Report by the UN and the Somali government (released in March)
a3681.speech: Said that drought might have led to 43,000 “excess deaths” last year, with children under the age of five accounting for half the victims.

a3681.speaker: Somali government
a3681.name: Somali government
a3681.speech: Said late last month that more than 3,000 Al-Shabaab fighters had been killed since it launched the offensive; also said 70 towns and villages had been “liberated” from Al-Shabaab.

a3681.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of Somalia
a3681.name: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud
a3681.title: President of Somalia
a3681.speech: Last year declared “all-out war” against the Islamists and sent in troops in September to back an uprising against Al-Shabaab launched by local clan militias in central Somalia.

a3863.speaker: Mwilima Mushokabanji, Meatco CEO
a3863.name: Mwilima Mushokabanji
a3863.title: Meatco CEO
a3863.speech: says the FMD outbreak was under control at the moment; assured the world, saying the country has the expertise and capacity to deal with the current FMD outbreak in the protection zone ; “We are confident that there is no risk of FMD being spread to the US through our beef produced,” adding that all beef exported to the US is procured from Namibia's free zone without vaccination, a zone that has been free without vaccination since 1965 ; said Namibia as a member of the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) subscribes to regular reporting and follow-up of diseases notifications ; “Namibia has a proven and audited animal disease surveillance system and in situations such as this is capable of early detection and reporting of animal diseases in any of the Namibian zones.” ; “It is important to stress that the reporting of such outbreak is not a sign of weakness in the system but rather a sign that the system is working effectively and can be relied upon.” ; said Namibia has an effective Livestock Identification and Traceability system with proven capabilities of forward and backwards tracing of livestock and livestock products ; “Namibia has a well-founded and demonstrative capacity to respond to FMD outbreaks without affecting trade, we justly, believe that Namibia has the expertise and capacity to deal with the current FMD outbreak in the protection zone without affecting the safe production of beef in the FMD free zone.” ; said the country does not rely on a single zoo sanitary measure to control FMD, rather it combines a number of OIE approved zoo sanitary measures ; “We are confident its free status is as a result of the assessments of all its interventions rather than focusing on a single intervention e.g. all levels of protection.”

a3863.speaker: United States Cattlemen's Association (USCA)
a3863.name: United States Cattlemen's Association (USCA)
a3863.speech: recently raised concerns about Namibia's beef and called on its government to halt with immediate effect beef imports from Namibia due to the FMD outbreak.

a3863.speaker: Thinus Pretorius, chairperson of the Livestock Producers Organisation (LPO) of Namibia
a3863.name: Thinus Pretorius
a3863.title: chairperson of the Livestock Producers Organisation (LPO) of Namibia
a3863.speech: shared similar sentiments as Mushokabanji, saying that Namibia has a disease-free, highly regulated and individually traceable livestock system ; “For approximately 60 years, the country has managed to be FMD-free due to the effective and stringent procedures put in place. This is an achievement of which Namibia is proud.” ; added that as a livestock producer, he can relate to the concerns of the USCA, because a possible FMD-outbreak south of the veterinary cordon fence (VCF) would spell disaster for the Namibian red meat industry ; “We will do everything in their power to uphold the free status. Various protocols are put in place by the competent authority to eliminate the risk of contamination, including inoculation north of the VCF, a surveillance area within the FMD-free zone with strict movement control, and strict procedures by export abattoirs regarding post-mortem tests and cooling of carcasses to eliminate any risks of virus infection.”

a3935.speaker: World Bank International Debt Report
a3935.name: World Bank International Debt Report
a3935.speech: Says developing nations across the globe, including Nigeria, spent $1.4 trillion to service foreign debt, climbing to a 20-year high in 2023; interest payments surged by nearly a third to $406 billion, squeezing the budgets of many countries in critical areas such as health, education, and the environment; the financial strain was fiercest among the poorest and most vulnerable countries eligible to borrow from the International Development Association (IDA), which paid a record $96.2 billion to service their debt in 2023, with interest costs surging to an all-time high of $34.6 billion — four times the amount a decade ago; interest payments of IDA countries now amount to nearly six percent of export earnings, a level not seen since 1999, and for some countries run as high as 38% of export earnings; the report added that since 2022, foreign private creditors have received nearly $13 billion more in debt-service payments from public sector borrowers in IDA-eligible economies than they disbursed in new financing, while the World Bank and other multilateral institutions pumped in nearly $51 billion more in 2022 and 2023 than they collected; the report also stressed that the COVID-19 pandemic sharply enlarged the debt burdens of all developing countries, with total external debt of low- and middle-income countries at a record $8.8 trillion at the end of 2023.

a3935.speaker: Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)
a3935.name: Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)
a3935.speech: According to the NBS, the country spent $3.5 billion or N120.01 billion on external debt servicing in 2023, reflecting a 54% rise from the N78 billion of 2022.

a3935.speaker: Indermit Gill, World Bank Group Chief Economist and Senior Vice President
a3935.name: Indermit Gill
a3935.title: World Bank Group Chief Economist and Senior Vice President
a3935.speech: “Multilateral institutions have become the last lifeline for poor economies struggling to balance debt payments with spending on health, education, and other key development priorities. In highly indebted poor countries, multilateral development banks are now acting as a lender of last resort, a role they were not designed to serve. That reflects a dysfunctional financing system: except for funds from the World Bank and other multilateral institutions, money is flowing out of poor economies when it should be flowing in.”

a3935.speaker: Haishan Fu, World Bank Chief Statistician and Director of its Development Data Group
a3935.name: Haishan Fu
a3935.title: World Bank Chief Statistician and Director of its Development Data Group
a3935.speech: “Comprehensive data on the liabilities of governments can facilitate new investment, reduce corruption, and prevent costly debt crises. The World Bank has played a leading role in improving debt transparency across the world, especially in IDA-eligible economies. In 2023, nearly 70% of these economies published fully accessible public-debt data on a government website—a 20-point increase since 2020. That is a hopeful sign for the future.”

a3967.speaker: Stakeholders, including development partners
a3967.name: Stakeholders
a3967.title: including development partners
a3967.speech: Have identified gaps in digital health transformation and proposed solutions to expedite Tanzania's move towards Universal Health Coverage.

a3967.speaker: Panelists at the USAID Public Sector Systems Strengthening Plus (USAID PS3+) Health Forum, Zanzibar
a3967.name: Panelists at the USAID Public Sector Systems Strengthening Plus (USAID PS3+) Health Forum
a3967.title: Zanzibar
a3967.speech: Emphasized the importance of collaboration between the public and private sectors; noted that effectively using strengthened systems is crucial for expanding healthcare coverage.

a3967.speaker: Dr Gemini Mtei, Deputy Chief of Party (DCOP) for the Abt-led USAID PS3+
a3967.name: Dr Gemini Mtei
a3967.title: Deputy Chief of Party (DCOP) for the Abt-led USAID PS3+
a3967.speech: Highlighted the need to strengthen digital platforms by investing in technology to facilitate the enrolment of individuals in health insurance schemes; said that as the government expands health insurance coverage, it is essential to develop systems capable of managing populations from the formal and informal sector down to the community level; stressed the importance of investing in digital transformation to create simple enrolment processes, potentially through mobile technology; noted that one of the main challenges that may discourage the willingness of people to enroll is the bureaucratic process of enrolment: "If the enrolment process is cumbersome, people are unlikely to register."

a3967.speaker: Dr Gemini Mtei, Deputy Chief of Party (DCOP) for the Abt-led USAID PS3+
a3967.name: Dr Gemini Mtei
a3967.title: Deputy Chief of Party (DCOP) for the Abt-led USAID PS3+
a3967.speech: Said that integrating electronic medical records with health insurance claims management systems is critical, allowing for a two-way management approach for services provided to insured members; added that a robust claims management system should include an audit trail to track member management across healthcare facilities; stressed the need for coordination with private providers to enhance the efficiency of the health insurance system and guarantee continuum of care; noted a current gap due to the absence of a national data set that can track a patient's journey from public to private facilities.

a3967.speaker: Silvanus Ilomo, Director of Information & Communication Technologies at the Ministry of Health (MOH), Tanzania
a3967.name: Silvanus Ilomo
a3967.title: Director of Information & Communication Technologies at the Ministry of Health (MOH), Tanzania
a3967.speech: Said that through USAID support and strong collaboration with key stakeholders, the MOH has been able to harmonize systems across the community: "In deploying digital systems like the Unified Community System (UCS), the ministry collaborates closely with stakeholders, including the private sector."

a3967.speaker: Ali Idrissa Abeid, Zanzibar Health Services Fund (ZHSF)
a3967.name: Ali Idrissa Abeid
a3967.title: Zanzibar Health Services Fund (ZHSF)
