I urge His Excellency, the President, to ignore this illicit public call by the GBA leadership as if same was never made, for it is a wrong call. It is better for a law to be wrong than for a wrong to be law."

a6930.speaker: Ghana Bar Association (GBA)
a6930.name: Ghana Bar Association (GBA)
a6930.speech: "The GBA has not yet responded to the allegations."

a6930.speaker: thelawplatform.online (report)
a6930.name: thelawplatform.online (report)
a6930.speech: Reported that the resolution calling on President Mahama to revoke the suspension of Chief Justice Torkornoo was passed at the GBA's Mid-Year Conference held at Labadi Beach Hotel in Accra on April 26, 2025, and indicated that members of the Bar were displeased with the suspension of the Chief Justice after getting details of the three petitions for her removal.

a6930.speaker: Members of the Ghana Bar Association
a6930.name: Members of the Ghana Bar Association
a6930.speech: Were not happy with the determination of a prima facie case in the three petitions filed for Justice Torkornoo's removal by President Mahama and the Council of State, and expressed their displeasure with the association's leadership over a statement issued regarding the ongoing process for removing the Chief Justice, indicating that they were not happy with the import and tone of the statement, which was dated April 24, 2025.

a6930.speaker: Ghana Bar Association (GBA)
a6930.name: Ghana Bar Association (GBA)
a6930.speech: Indicated that it would present a petition challenging the removal of the Chief Justice.

a6930.speaker: Bar Council of England and Wales
a6930.name: Bar Council of England and Wales
a6930.speech: Issued a statement condemning the suspension of Chief Justice Gertrude Araba Asaaba Sackey Torkornoo, which the Majority Chief Whip described as attacking the Ghanaian government "without provocation."

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Says the assessment of the 4th SIDS Summit is very positive: "we are talking about a very positive balance, a long process that unfolded over several months, including discussions that took place in Cabo Verde"; that, unlike many international summits where negotiations drag on, there was great convergence on the essential point of mobilising all efforts to support small island states facing unprecedented levels of vulnerability; that "Today, no one doubts that small island states are in a very difficult situation" - they suffer the most consequences from climate change, with these 39 countries representing two thirds of the countries most affected, and about 40% of small island states now have unsustainable debt levels or close to it; that convergence extended to how to act, through the 10-year ABAS Action Plan (Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS); that very important progress was achieved on the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, long demanded by SIDS, which will not replace GDP per capita but adds information; and that, unlike the three previous action plans, this plan will have evaluation, monitoring and reporting mechanisms and "is not a plan of the SIDS, it is a plan for the SIDS" - meaning the whole international community, including donors, will be assessed, which will create a very important level of accountability.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Says on financing that there are three decisive areas - supply, demand and the organisation of the market itself: more financing must be mobilised for the SIDS, more public financing, namely official development assistance, but also innovative mechanisms such as blended finance, impact investment, external credit lines, fiscal reforms at international level including eliminating fossil-fuel subsidies, and the development of carbon markets; "the SIDS will need, over the next 10 years, 70 billion dollars for infrastructure financing. At the moment, the SIDS receive about 3 or 4 billion dollars in official development assistance", so international public financing will not be enough and private investment must also be mobilised; on the demand side the small island states will have to carry out political and structural reforms to create a regulatory environment that attracts investment, including spatial planning and water-resources policies and reform of the remuneration of renewable energy; a third dimension is technical capacity, requiring cooperation partnerships to strengthen skills in project design and implementation; and the market for development finance itself must be reformed. He also highlights innovative financing and debt, noting that "the example of Cabo Verde was referred to in multiple questions... as a country that found an interesting, innovative solution for exchanging debt for investment in the green, blue and digital areas", mechanisms known in English as debt for climate and debt for nature.

a6936.speaker: United Nations Secretary-General
a6936.name: United Nations Secretary-General
a6936.speech: Has been advocating a reform of the international financial system so that the SIDS have more representation, more voice, more participation and more voting rights, so that more liquidity can be allocated to the SIDS and these agencies have more lending capacity.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Says Cabo Verde's bet on the green economy, the blue economy and digitalisation is "without doubt... the right agenda": the agenda of blue and green growth, in essence the decarbonisation agenda, not only to reduce emissions but to create jobs and companies in clean technologies, renewable energy and energy efficiency; the agenda of protecting the oceans while also valuing them economically, not only through traditional sectors such as fisheries but also new activities such as offshore energy and biotechnology; and the unavoidable digital agenda, which for SIDS that are so territorially disconnected is essential for equality of opportunity, for children's access to education, for a more transparent and less bureaucratic society and for trade, since digital commerce now carries great weight.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Says on attracting investment that the international community - public and private sector - must mobilise to support small island states not only out of solidarity but because it is a good, reproductive investment; that economic activity should be diversified rather than "putting all the eggs in the same basket", in tourism or fisheries or agriculture, and concentrated in the fastest-growing sectors such as the green economy; and recalls that "there are 460 trillion dollars available in the financial markets, in pension funds and in the capital market", so countries must do everything they can, through national policies and international diplomacy, to attract that financing, because there is global competition.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Declines to comment on Cabo Verde's national agendas - "I would prefer not to comment on national agendas, because there is a good rule, which is, obviously, that national policies are the responsibility of the countries, of democratically elected governments" - but says that from what he observes in international meetings, with the participation of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Foreign Affairs, it is evident that Cabo Verde is making itself felt in these international discussions, because it is not only demanding more international solidarity but also demonstrating a willingness to lead themes as important as the Digital Agenda, the Green Agenda and the Blue Agenda.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: Says the question of scale is not surmountable - it is the reality these countries must live with - but connectivity is, through transport, the digital component and trade; that scale makes investment more costly, and "we know, for example, that in official development assistance... when it comes to projects in small island states, the cost is four times higher", because of smaller scale, higher material costs, greater climate vulnerabilities and the need for more resilient infrastructure; that therefore the international community has "the moral obligation to mobilise to support these countries", because there are levels of vulnerability that are almost insurmountable; and that many SIDS have GDP per capita levels that made them no longer eligible or no longer a priority for development assistance - as with Cabo Verde, which graduated from least developed to middle-income country - even though such countries can lose everything in a natural disaster, as has frequently happened in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which is why the multidimensional vulnerability indicator matters so much for decision-makers in development agencies, donor countries, development banks and investment banks. He adds that this summit "achieved historic levels of convergence with the SIDS agenda. Now it is necessary to move to action", and that UN agencies such as UNOPS must be available for partnerships on the ground to help deliver projects, namely infrastructure.

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: On whether GDP per capita is a trap: "I don't know whether it is a trap. It has been a metric that has not been sufficiently robust to deal with the small states... GDP per capita, which will have to continue to be used for many decisions, cannot be the only metric. That is why this multidimensional vulnerability indicator is a good contribution."

a6936.speaker: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government), not named in the article text
a6936.name: Interviewed senior UN official (UNOPS; former member of the Portuguese government)
a6936.title: not named in the article text
a6936.speech: On whether the SIDS agenda can be delivered amid the emergence of extremist parties and governments less interested in international cooperation: "In an increasingly interdependent world, we all gain from greater solidarity with the most vulnerable. The solution to the great global problems lies in more multilateralism and more cooperation, and not in closure or intolerance."

a6936.speaker: Ulisses Correia e Silva, Prime Minister of Cabo Verde
a6936.name: Ulisses Correia e Silva
a6936.title: Prime Minister of Cabo Verde
a6936.speech: The Prime Minister of Cabo Verde, who was present at the Summit, spoke about the question of the SIDS' financing difficulties, and in his participation in the Summit argued that the SIDS have to escape the trap of GDP per capita.

a6942.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release / seasons message)
a6942.name: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release / seasons message)
a6942.speech: Has criticized what it calls the "hasty passage" of Liberia's national budget for the 2025 fiscal period by the Legislature, stating it violates critical Liberian laws and best practices ; noted that over the last two months the House of Representatives has been embroiled with leadership struggle, which has significantly hamstrung the conduct of legislative activities, including the timely submission of the fiscal year 2025 National Budget ; "we have seen nothing else from the people's representatives, but a clamor for power and control over the country's resources as well as claims and counterclaims of corruption." ; "During this period, perhaps worse than before, the lawmakers' personal interests have superseded public interest."

a6942.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.name: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.speech: Stressed that the review and discussion on the draft 2025 national budget and its passage happened in the period of ten days, and that deliberations were not presided over by the constitutionally-elected and sitting Speaker of the House of Representatives but by a faction of Representatives with no authority to do so; said anyone can clearly see the lack of scrutiny as the budget was passed with lightning speed, with seemingly no objections to proposals from the Executive ; "It is our opinion, that only an illegitimate faction of the House seeking favors and recognition from the Executive would proceed in such a manner that admits of no oversight."

a6942.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.name: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.speech: Said it is deeply troubled by several missteps associated with the 2025 national budget submission and review process, which undermine its transparency and credibility and may have further implications for allocations to critical sectors, institutions and programs; said the executive branch's submission of the draft budget on November 18, 2024 violates section 17.1 of the amended 2019 public financial management act ; "In short, the submission process did not meet the two-month timeline provided for by the public financial management law of Liberia, thus allowing little time for review, deliberations, and passage/approval by the Legislature." ; "Additionally, the 2025 National Budget did not undergo the required review and scrutiny, thus undermining its credibility and compliance with acceptable best practices and standards." ; "Besides, there is no publicly available information that the legislature thoroughly reviewed performance reports of the various spending entities, before approving their allocations in the current budget."

a6942.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.name: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.speech: Called on the Legislature to lead by example, as the direct representatives of the people, to set example of the adherence to the rule of law, including through respect for laid down procedures on deliberating on bills or removal of a sitting Speaker; said there can be no short-cut about rule of law and adherence to budgetary process, for all the mishaps could surely haunt the country in the not-too-distant future; emphasized that the actions of a certain group of lawmakers to assume the authority to pass the budget is a dangerous precedent as, going forward, any group of 38 lawmakers can gather together to make laws outside of established channels in so far as they have the backing of the Executive ; "We, therefore, call on President Joseph N. Boakai to distance himself from this illegal act by refusing to recognize same as a product of proper legislative enactment." ; "We believe that this would not only allay concerns that the Presidency has been actively involved in undermining the sitting Speaker, but that it would also serve to safeguard the integrity of our budget process."

a6942.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.name: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (press release)
a6942.speech: Has welcomed Liberia's eligibility for the MCC Grant, saying it is a boast to the image of the country, and applauds the Liberian government for achieving this milestone, which presents the country with an opportunity to leverage resources to fund infrastructure and other critical sectors that will spur inclusive and sustainable economic growth and development, if properly and inclusively managed ; "We thank the US Government, through MCC, for this initiative and partnership and call for timely information sharing as well as meaningful civil society and citizens' participation at all levels of Liberia's Compact development, implementation, and monitoring processes." ; "We urge that successes, challenges, and lessons learned from the country's past Compact inform decision-making around the new partnership, to ensure greater transparency, accountability, and inclusion of citizens and CSOs' voices."

a6942.speaker: Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a6942.name: Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a6942.speech: Announced, during its quarterly meeting on December 18, Liberia's eligibility and selection for a new Compact, following the end of the previous compact in 2021, in recognition of the progress the country has made to strengthen its performance on the MCC scorecard and the country's commitment to pursuing critical economic and democratic governance reforms.

a6942.speaker: Press Bureau of the House of Representatives of Liberia (dispatch)
a6942.name: Press Bureau of the House of Representatives of Liberia (dispatch)
a6942.speech: Reported that about five days after deliberations began, on Friday, December 13, 2024, the revenue component of the budget debate was exhausted.

a7071.speaker: Dr. Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister of Finance
a7071.name: Dr. Mwigulu Nchemba
a7071.title: Minister of Finance
a7071.speech: Presented the budget framework and expenditure ceiling for the 2025/26 financial year to the Parliamentary Budget Committee in Dodoma: "The 2025/26 budget will be financed by TZS 40.97 trillion in revenue and TZS 16.07 trillion from domestic and foreign loans. This includes TZS 31.83 trillion from tax revenue, TZS 6.23 trillion from non-tax revenue, TZS 1.68 trillion from local government revenues, and TZS 1.22 trillion from grants." ; He emphasized that the budget will support the final phase of the 2025 Development Vision and the 2025/26 Development Plan, with key spending priorities including debt servicing, the government wage bill, the general elections, strengthening democracy, maintaining peace and security, and preparations for the AFCON 2027 tournament.

a7071.speaker: Prof. Kitila Mkumbo, Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment
a7071.name: Prof. Kitila Mkumbo
a7071.title: Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment
a7071.speech: Addressed concerns about declining aid from developed nations and reassured the parliamentary committee that the government is prepared to mitigate the impact of reduced foreign aid: "We are strengthening alternative financing mechanisms, such as public-private partnerships, to increase private sector participation in the economy. Honorable Members of Parliament need not worry. The government is fully committed to ensuring that reduced foreign aid strengthens our self-reliance and efficiency."

a7143.speaker: Arnaud Rugema, representative of CRDB Bank Burundi
a7143.name: Arnaud Rugema
a7143.title: representative of CRDB Bank Burundi
a7143.speech: "We have come to the residents of Gatumba affected by the floods to show them that they are not alone." ; specified that the aid, consisting of 3 tonnes of rice, 3 tonnes of beans, sorghum, exercise books for 480 pupils and 500 kitchen utensil kits, as well as financial assistance, is the fruit of the fundraising carried out during the CRDB Marathon 2024, which made it possible to raise more than 100 million Burundian francs ; "This initiative will take place every year and CRDB Bank Burundi is ready to support anyone who wishes to develop empowerment projects at the Gateri site."

a7143.speaker: Pamphile Hakizimana, administrator of Buganda commune
a7143.name: Pamphile Hakizimana
a7143.title: administrator of Buganda commune
a7143.speech: Expressed his deep gratitude to CRDB Bank Burundi and its partners for their action on behalf of the disaster victims: "These families live thanks to humanitarian aid because they no longer have land to cultivate," he stressed ; strongly encouraged the beneficiaries to use this assistance to start small income-generating activities, such as trade, in order to begin their gradual reconstruction.

a7143.speaker: Raphaël Nijimbere, speaking on behalf of the families rehoused at Gateri
a7143.name: Raphaël Nijimbere
a7143.title: speaking on behalf of the families rehoused at Gateri
a7143.speech: Warmly thanked the donors for their generosity and the communal authorities for their support in their resettlement: "We are grateful to you for what you have brought us, as well as to the authorities of Buganda commune who showed us how to settle in. We request your continued support so that you plead our cause so that we may benefit from vocational training, learn agricultural techniques, and so that the government helps us obtain arable land to ensure our subsistence." ; concluded by asking for the assistance of construction experts to build durable housing, given the rocky nature of the site, which makes digging difficult without appropriate equipment.

a7241.speaker: Daniel Bertossa, General Secretary of Public Services International (PSI)
a7241.name: Daniel Bertossa
a7241.title: General Secretary of Public Services International (PSI)
a7241.speech: Said at the protest demonstration: "We are in a very difficult and unfortunate situation, in which it is not only the world's governments that are being attacked, but also the UN and its agencies."

a7241.speaker: EFE (news agency)
a7241.name: EFE (news agency)
a7241.speech: According to the EFE news agency, the situation is being aggravated by the withdrawal of a large part of the aid from its main contributor, the government of the United States.

a7241.speaker: Severine Deboos, President of the staff union of the International Labour Organization (ILO)
a7241.name: Severine Deboos
a7241.title: President of the staff union of the International Labour Organization (ILO)
a7241.speech: Added: "We are not a commodity, but human beings who have a right to good working conditions and to respect for our dignity."

a7241.speaker: Organisers of the demonstration
a7241.name: Organisers of the demonstration
a7241.speech: Said that, following the drastic cut in US aid, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have reduced staff worldwide by around 30%, while the ILO cut 10% of its jobs.

a7241.speaker: Nathalie Meynet and Cristina Pierini, leaders of CCISUA and FICSA
a7241.name: Nathalie Meynet and Cristina Pierini
a7241.title: leaders of CCISUA and FICSA
a7241.speech: Said: "These are not just statistics; behind them are thousands of people who deliver humanitarian aid, ensure access to drinking water, food and health care, protect refugees and displaced people, keep children in school, prevent forced labour and defend human rights."

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Explained PDOIS' alternative economic policy required to transform The Gambia, disclosing to members the state of the Gambian economy by highlighting the role of the central bank. He said the Central Bank of the Gambia is the most important institution today: "It is the depository of public wealth and relies on taxation and other sources of revenue to put in its coffers. It determines the monetary policy, supervises other (commercial) banks and insurance companies to ensure that investment goes to the productive base of the economy."

a7253.speaker: Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of The Gambia (quoted by Halifa Sallah)
a7253.name: Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of The Gambia (quoted by Halifa Sallah)
a7253.speech: Indicated last year that the net foreign assets of the country and the central bank are plunging ; according to the Minister, industry in 2023 constituted construction, electricity, mining at quarries, etc.

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Said Gambia is exporting only groundnuts, cashew nuts and fish to countries like the United Kingdom, India and Turkey, generating about 270 million dollars, while importing rice, other cereals, oil and electricity from Senegal at a cost of over 700 million dollars: "Therefore, the earning capacity is in a state of deficit which impacts on the foreign assets of our central bank. We become captives of the IMF because of a deficit needing a loan for a balance of payments support." ; "Consequently, we have duty waivers amounting to over 2 billion dalasi in 2022 and over 3.9 billion dalasi in 2023. So, how can wealth increase?" ; "That is why borrowing has increased, requiring 7.5 billion dalasi in debt service in 2024. That is the state of our economy." ; said that must change, and noted that other than the agrarian economy there must also be industrial development, which only contributes 20% of GDP.

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: "PDOIS is saying invest in the productive base through the accumulation of Sovereign National wealth. We are a country of 11,285 square kilometres of territory; land, sea and air belong to us. Whatever is there in wealth is sovereign National Wealth. That is what PDOIS is telling you. We own that. That is why we fought for liberation and got rid of the colonialist so that we can take ownership of our land." ; "What justification can we give to a Gambian who wants land and cannot get land? Do we call ourselves liberated if we want land and cannot get land in our homeland? That will never happen under a PDOIS government." ; "We say foreign direct investment; in other areas of our economy, but not to take over the land of our people, employ women who grow the vegetables and get paid starvation wages."

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Said the question PDOIS has ever asked is, "can we feed ourselves?", and said PDOIS is saying invest in the productive base so that agricultural produce can be transformed into value added products: "We will produce our own soap, milk, all sorts of needed products. It is possible to do it in small and large scale by ensuring those who want to engage in processing these agricultural produce can get the type of support needed. Employment will be generated. Import lowered and production enhanced."

a7253.speaker: Minister of Agriculture of The Gambia (quoted by Halifa Sallah)
a7253.name: Minister of Agriculture of The Gambia (quoted by Halifa Sallah)
a7253.speech: Once quoted what PDOIS has indicated in its manifesto, that there is 550,000 hectares of land available for cultivation.

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Said the country is being informed about mining in Batukunku, Sanyang and Kartong but what is being generated is unknown, and stressed the need to have a system where everything owned will be in sovereign hands.

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: "The government elected will see to it that there is a country divided into regions, each region developed. The starting point of development is the villages. Each village will have a village development committee to help villagers understand their earning capacity which will be retained at the village level. It does not leave." ; said the village/ward development plan will form the body of the annual national budget so that all parts of the country are developed together and there will be no rural-urban drift or migration to other parts of the world; said that is what the law of balanced and proportionate development of society is about, a policy which never existed, under which the wealth of the country will be distributed according to the needs of the people and which will eradicate poverty, while the current system he argued increases poverty.

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Concluded his deliberation on the state of the economy with an advice to PDOIS members that "they should not allow the party to be judged by the number of seats in parliament, councils or election results. Those doing that are looking at history with the wrong lenses. PDOIS is interested in changing lives and livelihoods of its people. Those who want to be part of the journey should know the history. PDOIS has been an asset to this country and all other political parties."

a7253.speaker: Halifa Sallah, Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.name: Halifa Sallah
a7253.title: Secretary General of PDOIS
a7253.speech: Moved on to the constitutional reform process, which he said started in 2017.

a7268.speaker: The Lancet medical journal (editorial and paper)
a7268.name: The Lancet medical journal (editorial and paper)
a7268.speech: According to a Lancet editorial about a simultaneously-launched global health initiative to prevent 100 million deaths from heart attacks and strokes in LMICs within the next 30 years; according to the Lancet paper, dietary sodium, or salt, is a major contributor to high blood pressure which in turn places a person at significant risk of developing heart disease; the Lancet paper noted that reducing salt intake can help prevent and manage high blood pressure but access to medicines, currently cheap across the world, are also needed to save lives; and noted in the Lancet, “[f]ewer than one in six people live in countries implementing these three key interventions”.

a7268.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a7268.name: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a7268.speech: According to the WHO, cardiovascular diseases are “a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels” and 80% of the resulting deaths are caused by heart attacks and strokes; the WHO recommends 5g of salt per day.

a7268.speaker: Dr Tom Frieden, Resolve's president and co-author of the Lancet paper
a7268.name: Dr Tom Frieden
a7268.title: Resolve's president and co-author of the Lancet paper
a7268.speech: “There are proven strategies every country can use to prevent deaths from heart disease, stroke and epidemics - but progress has been painfully slow,” said Dr Tom Frieden in a statement, adding that strategic investments in three areas, “increasing global control of blood pressure, sodium reduction, and eliminating artificial trans fats - could deliver rapid progress”.

a7268.speaker: Resolve (global health initiative housed at Vital Strategies)
a7268.name: Resolve (global health initiative housed at Vital Strategies)
a7268.speech: Resolve's aim is to reduce global sodium intake by 30%; according to Resolve trans-fats cause over half a million deaths globally a year and they are calling for their total elimination in foods; according to Resolve only 14% of the 1.4 billion people on the planet with high blood pressure have it under control, placing them at risk of stroke, heart attacks, kidney damage and other health issues.

a7268.speaker: International research (cited)
a7268.name: International research (cited)
a7268.speech: According to international research, high blood pressure kills more people globally than any other single condition - resulting in the deaths of about 10 million people a year.

a7268.speaker: Michael Bloomberg, philanthropist and former New York mayor
a7268.name: Michael Bloomberg
a7268.title: philanthropist and former New York mayor
a7268.speech: “The world’s leading cause of death is largely preventable, and we can’t sit back while people suffer needlessly. We know what measures are proven to help reduce sickness and death from cardiovascular diseases. Every step we take to spread those measures will make a difference. Saving 100 million lives would be an extraordinary achievement - and it’s within our reach.”

a7269.speaker: Jackson Mvuganyi, host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.name: Jackson Mvuganyi
a7269.title: host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.speech: Shared his insight on the GTV Breakfast show on the upcoming U.S. presidential election and its potential effects on Africa, saying this election holds significant importance for African nations, especially in areas like trade, security, health, climate, and diplomatic relationships; noted that in recent years global powers, including the U.S., China, and Russia, have shown increased interest in Africa, recognising its growing economic influence, young population, and rich resources.

a7269.speaker: Jackson Mvuganyi, host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.name: Jackson Mvuganyi
a7269.title: host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.speech: Explained that if the next U.S. administration chooses to extend or expand the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which is set to expire in 2025, it could boost African economies, while on the other hand a more protectionist U.S. trade approach could reduce these benefits.

a7269.speaker: Jackson Mvuganyi, host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.name: Jackson Mvuganyi
a7269.title: host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.speech: Noted that the next U.S. president's decisions on health funding, including through initiatives like the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and support for global health organizations, will directly affect Africa's health systems.

a7269.speaker: Jackson Mvuganyi, host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.name: Jackson Mvuganyi
a7269.title: host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.speech: Stressed that U.S. support for climate action and green energy projects in Africa is essential to help the continent address its environmental challenges.

a7269.speaker: Jackson Mvuganyi, host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.name: Jackson Mvuganyi
a7269.title: host of the Voice of America red carpet show
a7269.speech: Said the U.S. election outcome could shape the continent's geopolitical landscape, especially as the U.S. competes with other countries like China and Russia for influence in Africa, and believes that although U.S. election debates have largely focused on domestic issues, the results will still impact Africa's economy, security, and international alliances.

a7301.speaker: Dr. Amadou Hamadoun Dicko, teacher-researcher and senior lecturer in microbial biotechnology, University of Segou (class patron)
a7301.name: Dr. Amadou Hamadoun Dicko
a7301.title: teacher-researcher and senior lecturer in microbial biotechnology, University of Segou (class patron)
a7301.speech: Said he was very moved by his students' decision to associate his name with the class: "I want to express to them all my gratitude for this consideration. It means that I must redouble my efforts in my mission of training the country's future leaders."

a7301.speaker: Dr. Amadou Hamadoun Dicko, teacher-researcher and senior lecturer in microbial biotechnology, University of Segou (class patron)
a7301.name: Dr. Amadou Hamadoun Dicko
a7301.title: teacher-researcher and senior lecturer in microbial biotechnology, University of Segou (class patron)
a7301.speech: Urged the new graduates to continue their efforts in order to meet the professional challenges awaiting them: "I advised them to work tirelessly so as to serve their country with honour and dedication, and to keep improving in order to be competitive on the national and international market."

a7464.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.speech: Has recorded, over the last month, a worsening humanitarian crisis caused by funding shortages, natural disasters and escalating armed violence in the northern Mozambican province of Cabo Delgado: "Escalation of violence by Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG) continued to drive displacement, disrupt essential services, severely restrict movement, exacerbate food insecurity, and enable the delivery of life-saving assistance".

a7464.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.speech: "On 24 June, 568 individuals, including 324 children, fled NSAG attacks in Quinto Congresso village towards the already overcrowded Macomia district headquarters", bringing "the total number of people displaced by conflict to 48,000 since 1 January".

a7464.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a7464.speech: Acknowledges that the Mozambican government has facilitated returns in Macomia, Metuge, and Montepuez in Cabo Delgado, and recently in Mecula, Niassa, "largely driven by inadequate humanitarian assistance and overcrowding in sites for internally displaced people"; "The returnees found nothing in their areas of origin as their homes, agricultural plots and livelihoods were destroyed and basic services have not been restored. Those who opted for resettlement found the proposed sites lacking in essential services. The lack of response to returns heightens vulnerabilities and protection risks".

a7464.speech: Pointed to persistent "post-cyclone needs and gaps" as a major challenge: "With funding constraints, people affected by the three recent cyclones, which, in addition to destroying thousands of homes and infrastructure, caused around 175 deaths in the north and centre of the country, still require adequate assistance." ; "The first assessments conducted since March in Lalaua and Muecate districts in Nampula revealed that a combined 70,000 people were affected by the cyclones but have not received assistance since March".
